summary: Suggests strategies for using SIP and XMPP together in clients and servers, mainly with configuration changes and small software changes, taking telephony from SIP and messaging and presence from XMPP. It defines no new protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: Two chat tools each good at something are used together like a phone and a texting app.

subtitle: Strategies for combining SIP for calls and XMPP for messaging in one service.

tldr.problem: SIP excels at voice and video calling while XMPP excels at instant messaging and presence. Deploying a unified real-time communication service requires both, but they are separate protocols with different designs and user experiences.
tldr.mechanism: CUSAX (Combined Use of SIP and XMPP) suggests strategies for configuring clients and servers to use SIP exclusively for telephony features and XMPP exclusively for messaging, presence, and contact management. Configuration, discovery, and linking mechanisms allow a single service and account to transparently use both protocols.
tldr.outcome: Users get a unified communication experience: telephony from SIP's strength, instant messaging and presence from XMPP's strength, all in one client connecting to a single CUSAX service. No new protocols are defined; the document provides practical guidance for implementation.

facts.label: Default behavior
facts.value: SIP for calls, XMPP for messaging

facts.label: Contact linking
facts.value: vCard tel field for SIP URI

today: RFC 7081 is informational guidance for unified communications services that combine SIP and XMPP. It remains relevant for services implementing dual-protocol platforms, though it is not a standard and does not mandate implementation. Many commercial and open-source communication platforms have adopted CUSAX concepts.

sections.title: Why Combine SIP and XMPP
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) was designed for voice and video calling, and remains the best choice for telephony-like services. The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) was designed for instant messaging and user presence (knowing who is online), and remains the best choice for those services. Both protocols have been extended to support the other's features, but in practice, SIP is still preferred for calls and XMPP is still preferred for messaging.

Real-time communication services increasingly want both capabilities. A service provider deploying a unified communications platform can use CUSAX to combine them. Users connect to both a SIP server (for calling) and an XMPP server (for messaging and presence) as part of the same service, typically operated by the same provider. The key challenge is making this seamless for users and developers, rather than forcing them to manually manage two separate protocols.

This document provides practical strategies for implementing CUSAX in clients and servers. It does not define new protocols, but instead explains how to configure existing SIP and XMPP implementations to work together effectively.
sections.plainLanguage: One company runs a phone service and a chat service. This explains how to glue them together so users see just one app.

sections.title: Client Setup and Account Linking
sections.content:
A CUSAX client must manage two accounts: a SIP account for voice and video, and an XMPP account for messaging and presence. Service providers should offer online provisioning (such as a web portal) so users can configure both accounts at once with minimal input (typically just a username and password). The client then maintains both connections independently.

By default, CUSAX clients should disable calling features in XMPP and disable messaging features in SIP, so each protocol is used for what it does best. This avoids confusion and ensures compatibility with other XMPP and SIP users who may only support one protocol. The client may present these as separate Telephony and Chat connections to help users understand why they see two statuses.

To make calling work seamlessly, the XMPP server should populate a vCard for each user with a SIP URI (phone number or address) in the "tel" field. When a CUSAX user looks at their XMPP contact list, they can then click a "Call" button to initiate a SIP call, even though they are viewing XMPP contact information.
sections.plainLanguage: Sign up once, get both a phone number and a chat account. The app talks to both services but hides the complexity.

sections.title: Discovering and Linking Accounts
sections.content:
CUSAX clients must determine which SIP and XMPP accounts belong together. When a client is provisioned with only one calling-capable account (the SIP account), it should initiate calls directly without asking users to choose an account. This simplifies the user experience: users click "Call" and the client uses the obvious SIP account.

The client can indicate a formal CUSAX relationship between accounts, such as alice@xmpp.example.com and alice@sip.example.com. When no relationship is explicitly configured, the client can use information from vCards or XMPP presence announcements to discover connections. However, the client must verify any discovered relationship through trusted means (such as directory data or mutual vCard references) to prevent spoofing attacks.

When receiving an incoming SIP call, a CUSAX client can extract the caller's identity from the SIP Call-Info header (which may contain an XMPP address with purpose="impp") and then match it to a contact in the user's XMPP roster. This helps users transition from a call to text chat without re-identifying the contact.
sections.plainLanguage: The client figures out which phone number goes with which chat user, so it can show the caller's chat name when they call.

sections.title: Group Calls and Conferences
sections.content:
CUSAX supports both SIP audio/video conferences and XMPP Multi-User Chat (MUC) rooms. When a user joins an audio conference, the conference can advertise an associated MUC room for text chat. Similarly, a MUC room can advertise a SIP URI for audio/video interaction. Both function independently; a participant might be in the SIP call but not the MUC room, or vice versa.

The CUSAX client must clearly indicate which form of communication each participant supports (voice, text, or both) since not all participants may be in both. For example, a single-stack user might join only the SIP conference or only the MUC room. Service providers can implement tighter integration by mirroring roles, permissions, and mutes between the two, but this is optional and up to implementers.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference call can have a chat room for side conversations. Some people might call but not chat, or chat but not call.

sections.title: Security and Federation Challenges
sections.content:
A critical risk in CUSAX is security mismatch. The SIP aspect and XMPP aspect might use different authentication methods (SIP often uses digest authentication, XMPP often uses SCRAM or client certificates) or different TLS cipher suites. If only one aspect is protected by TLS encryption, users might believe the entire session is secure when it is not. This opens the door to downgrade attacks, eavesdropping, and information leakage.

Service providers must enforce consistent, strong security policies across both protocols. If both aspects cannot offer the same level of protection, the client must inform the user and allow them to increase security or disconnect. Implementers must reference the detailed security considerations in the SIP and XMPP specifications themselves.

Federation adds complexity. When a CUSAX user communicates with users at other domains that may only support SIP or only XMPP, calls might be routed differently or incur unexpected costs (such as PSTN charges). Service providers should use UI warnings and auditory cues to alert users to unusual situations, such as when a call might be billed or when features are unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone part uses encryption but the chat part does not, spies could read your messages. Both have to be equally safe or users need a warning.
